served.stem: Where are the four complexes of the electron transport chain located in a eukaryotic cell?
served.bankWhy: A proton gradient needs a membrane that protons cannot leak across, and only one mitochondrial membrane qualifies. Its folds, the cristae, pack far more chain complexes and ATP synthase into the same volume. Picture the pumps set into that folded wall, pushing protons out into the intermembrane space.

answer.line: The chain builds a proton gradient, and only the inner membrane is tight enough to hold one.

steps: Start from the job. The chain pumps H+ to build a gradient, and a gradient needs a wall protons cannot leak through.
Only one membrane qualifies. The outer membrane is full of porins and leaks. The inner membrane is tight, and its folds, the cristae, hold complexes I to IV and ATP synthase.
So all four complexes sit in the inner membrane. I, III and IV pump H+ from the matrix into the intermembrane space.

choices.note: Glycolysis runs in the cytosol, so it sounds close. The chain needs a sealed membrane, and the cytosol has none.
H+ gets pumped into this space, which is why it pulls. The pumps sit in the membrane beside it.
The one tight, folded membrane. The only place a gradient can be built and held.
The matrix holds most Krebs enzymes. The one exception, succinate dehydrogenase, is complex II, and it sits in the inner membrane too.
Porins let small molecules through the outer membrane, so it cannot hold a proton gradient.

student.lockIt: A gradient needs a tight membrane. In mitochondria, that is the inner membrane.
